name: reject-delimiter-sealed-contentname
description: An unlock request carrying a blob that WAS SEALED under a contentName with the binding delimiter inside it. THE ATTACK. sealed.contentKeys carries "body|text" beside the two honest coordinates, and the blob under it is one no run of this sealer produced: it was sealed under "dca-bind-v1|c|" + renderId + "|body|text" by a publisher that never ran the ban on the name it was handed. That is a CMS that skipped the name check, a second implementation of the sealer, or markup written by hand, and once such a blob is on a page, anyone who can read the page can post it back. It carries the same ephemeral point as the honest bodytext blob beside it, so an issuer agrees the same wrapping key from either, and the value it was sealed under is the only thing between opening it and not. WHY A BANNING ISSUER REFUSES IT. A content binding is four fields - "dca-bind-v1", "c", the renderId and the contentName - joined on the delimiter. Structural admission rejects a name carrying that character before policy, BIND construction or private-key work. WHAT AN IMPLEMENTATION THAT SKIPS THE BAN HANDS THE ATTACKER: the key. It joins the four fields it was handed, arrives at the exact string this blob was sealed under, the tag VERIFIES, and vYZegsRp8YfEF07iU63Ct15wjcEaITGXvuDMDZuzk3E comes back under a name expected.keys does not list. The matching honest-blob vector proves the same admission happens regardless of blob contents. This sealed-at vector additionally records the key a blind delimiter join would release, so it distinguishes structural admission from an implementation that merely tries authentication at the malformed name. A CONFORMANT ISSUER rejects the whole request with binding_failed and returns no key or error member. NOT CONFORMANT: reaching the private key, or returning a key of any kind under that name. THE VALUE IS ON RECORD, in `sealedUnder`: the coordinate the blob was sealed at, the exact string it was sealed under, and the key inside it. A replayer cannot rebuild that string, because its own builder refuses the field that carries the delimiter, which is the whole of what this vector pins. So the string is recorded, and with it a replay can open the blob, see a real key at a real coordinate rather than damaged bytes, and hold what it recovers to the key recorded here. REPLAY. Post `rawBody` VERBATIM - the string as it sits in this file, never a re-serialization of it - to the unlock endpoint, with `issuer` as the key material the issuer holds for its own name and keyId, and `publisher.signingKeys` as the public verification halves, read straight from this file rather than resolved by a deployment lookup. A pass is: expected.code where there is one; key material back for exactly the coordinates in expected.keys and no others; and an error back for exactly the coordinates in expected.errors, under the codes recorded there. No publisher private key is in this file, on purpose: an issuer never holds one, so everything a reject vector asks for is checkable with what a real issuer has. HOW FAR THE REFUSAL REACHES IS PART OF WHAT IS PINNED, and expected.privateKeyReached says which side of the line this body lands on. A request that fails integrity - a signature that does not verify, a signed resource with no renderId to bind to - has asked nothing that could be answered, so it is refused whole and before the key store is consulted at all. A blob presented at a coordinate it was not sealed at is one bad blob in an ordinary request: the only way to find out is to try it, so the key store is reached, the blob comes back as an error, and everything else the request carried is answered beside it. The untouched coordinates were never the attack, and a page has to keep working around one bad blob, so they are answered. Everything in the body but the attack is the render this vector was cut from - the envelope, the periodKeys section and the untouched blobs are what the publisher emitted. An unchanged regeneration retains the valid resourceJWT signature segment inside rawBody, so the body is byte-stable with seal-ecdh.json. A fresh seal still draws a new k, which is why a replayer verifies the segment rather than comparing it. The token is the one in the base vector from the same run, byte for byte, except in reject-no-renderid, reject-renderid-noncanonical and reject-renderid-wrong-width, whose envelopes are second tokens signed over resources with the renderId removed, given a noncanonical spelling, or resized, which is each vector's whole subject; in reject-forged-resourcejwt, whose signature segment was drawn by a key the publisher does not hold; in reject-tampered-resourcejwt, which carries the seal-ecdh token's own signature segment under a payload edited after signing; and in the two reject-alg-substituted arms, which carry that token's payload segment under a header rewritten to name another algorithm, with a third segment that is empty or a MAC - neither of which moves between runs.
